sections.title: From soft clay to a useful vessel
paragraphs: A potter starts with clay that contains enough water to be shaped. Water allows particles to move past one another when pressure is applied, so a lump can be stretched into a wall or compressed into a base. A form that stands when it is wet is not necessarily ready for the next stage. Its weight is carried by material that can still change shape. A narrow foot or a heavy upper edge may cause the wall to lean while the clay remains soft. In deciding how to shape a piece, the maker therefore has to consider both the object that is intended and the temporary material that will support it during making.

As a vessel dries, its shape and size change. Water leaves its surface first, and the material shrinks as it loses moisture. A thin edge can dry faster than a thick base. If the edge has already become firm while the base is still shrinking, the two parts may pull against one another. Covering the vessel loosely can slow the loss of water and allow the difference between the parts to become smaller. The cover is not needed forever. It is used to control the pace of drying while the material is at risk of shrinking unevenly. A piece that dries slowly can still crack if its parts have been joined badly.

Joining two pieces of clay is easier when both are at a similar stage of drying. A handle that is much wetter than the body may later shrink more than the place to which it was attached. Before joining them, a maker can roughen the surfaces and apply a thin mixture of clay and water known as slip. This helps the surfaces make contact rather than remaining two smooth faces pressed together. The angle and thickness of the attachment also matter. A well-made joint has to survive handling after firing, but it must first survive the much earlier movement that occurs as the pieces dry.

A potter may test the feel of the clay as it becomes firm. At an intermediate stage, a wall can support itself while still being soft enough to trim. This state is often described as leather-hard. The maker can turn the vessel over and remove material from its base without collapsing the walls. Trimming too early can deform the piece. Leaving it until it is completely dry can make cutting difficult and increase the risk of breaking an edge. Recognising the state of the material by touch and resistance can therefore be more reliable than assuming that a fixed number of hours will suit every piece.

The permanent change takes place when the clay is fired. Heating to a suitable temperature changes the material so that ordinary wetting cannot return it to workable clay. The result depends on the kind of clay and the firing conditions. Some fired clay remains porous, allowing water to enter small spaces in its structure. Other bodies become much denser at the temperatures for which they were prepared. A glaze can produce a surface with different properties from the underlying body. This separation between the surface and the body is useful: a vessel can have a durable outer finish while still requiring careful choice of the clay beneath it.

A fired object often carries clues about earlier work. A crack near a handle might have begun while the two parts were drying, even if it became obvious only after firing. A difference in thickness can help explain why a region changed temperature more slowly than another. Nevertheless, a single mark is rarely enough to establish what happened. An observer can look at the position of the mark, check whether related marks occur on other pieces and compare the result with a record of the process. This is why a useful workshop record describes both the preparation and the firing instead of treating the firing as the only stage worth recording.

Clay work is sometimes described by listing operations in order: shape, dry and fire. That sequence is useful, but it does not explain the decisions within each operation. The material suitable for adding a handle may be unsuitable for trimming a base, and the temperature suitable for one clay may be unsuitable for another. Each stage changes the possibilities available at the next one. By checking moisture, support and the intended use of the object, a potter can plan for these changes. The finished vessel then records a chain of choices, many of which were made long before the object first entered the kiln.

sections.title: Why some seeds wait
paragraphs: A seed can remain inactive even when it is alive. This is different from a seed that has died and can no longer grow. In some cases, a living seed would begin to germinate as soon as conditions became favourable. In others, a barrier within the seed must change before growth can begin. The difference is important for anyone testing a collection of seeds. If none grows in a tray, the result may indicate unsuitable conditions, an internal barrier, or loss of viability. The absence of a seedling is an observation, but it does not by itself decide which explanation is correct. A useful test considers those possibilities separately.

Water is needed in the first stages of germination. A dry seed can swell as it takes up water, and that uptake helps start processes required for growth. However, some seeds have a coat that strongly limits the passage of water. In such a case, placing the seed on damp material may leave its interior dry. A small opening in the coat can allow water to reach it. This is one reason a treatment that damages only the coat can sometimes promote germination. The treatment needs care because a deeper cut could harm the living tissue. The aim is to change the barrier, rather than to cut into the developing plant.

Other seeds can take up water without beginning to grow immediately. The delay can depend on the internal state of the seed rather than on the coat alone. For some species, exposure to a cool and moist period changes that state. A seed that passes through such a period in the soil may then respond when conditions warm. The order matters. A warm period alone need not have the same effect as warmth following cold. In a controlled test, the investigator can therefore compare groups that receive the same final conditions but have different prior treatment. The comparison helps reveal whether the earlier period made a difference.

Light can also affect the response of certain seeds. A small seed close to the soil surface may receive a different signal from one buried more deeply. Yet testing light requires attention to other differences between those positions. A seed beneath the surface may also experience different moisture and temperature. If the aim is to isolate light, a comparison should keep the other conditions as similar as possible. One group can be covered with an opaque material while another receives light under comparable conditions. The outcome would then say more about that specific signal than a simple comparison between seeds planted at two different depths.

The timing of germination has consequences after growth begins. A seedling is exposed to conditions that an intact seed can sometimes survive. If growth begins during a brief warm interval followed by damaging cold, the early start may offer little advantage. Waiting can reduce that risk, but it can also shorten the time available to establish roots or compete for light. The useful response is therefore tied to the conditions in which a species normally establishes itself. The writer regards the delay as a feature with possible costs and benefits. Describing all delayed seeds as defective would miss the role that timing can play.

Differences among seeds in a single collection can complicate the result. A group can include seeds that germinate quickly, seeds that require treatment and seeds that are no longer alive. An average time calculated only from the seeds that grew says nothing directly about how many failed to grow. Reporting the number that germinated alongside the timing makes it easier to interpret the observation. It also helps distinguish a treatment that speeds growth in a few seeds from one that enables many more seeds to grow. These outcomes answer different questions, although each could be described informally as an improvement in germination.

A practical trial starts by deciding which explanation it is intended to test. If a coat may block water, measuring whether seeds swell can offer information before any seedlings appear. If a prior cool period is suspected, the study can keep the final conditions the same and change the history of one group. Repeating observations under recorded conditions makes the findings easier to interpret and compare. No test removes every uncertainty, especially when the history of the seeds is unknown. It can, however, replace a broad claim that the seeds failed with a more useful account of which conditions produced growth and which possibilities remain open.

sections.title: Designing a queue for uncertain arrivals
paragraphs: A queue forms when the rate at which people want service is greater, for a time, than the rate at which they can be served. It can form even where total capacity is more than adequate over a whole day. A small counter might stand idle early in the morning and become crowded shortly afterwards. An average taken over both periods would conceal the conditions during the busiest interval. A design that assumes arrivals are evenly spaced could therefore produce too little room or too few staff when people actually need them. The important question is how arrivals and service interact over time, rather than which of their daily totals is larger.

The time needed to serve each person can vary as much as the time between arrivals. At an information desk, a simple request for directions may be answered quickly. Another visitor may need help comparing several routes, which can occupy the desk for longer. If both visitors use the same desk, the longer request affects the wait experienced by those who follow. The average service time provides some information about the workload, but it does not describe the longest interruption that the desk might experience. Observing the spread of service times helps explain why a queue can grow rapidly even on a day with an ordinary number of arrivals.

When several desks offer the same service, a shared line can direct the next person to whichever desk becomes free. In separate lines, a visitor may be left behind a complicated request while another desk is already serving people who arrived later. A shared line reduces that particular risk, but it can take up a different shape of space. It may be harder to fit beside a narrow entrance. Separate lines can be appropriate if the desks actually offer different services and visitors can identify the right one. The writer therefore regards the physical arrangement and the differences between services as part of the choice, rather than treating one layout as universally best.

A separate appointment system changes the nature of the queue without necessarily eliminating it. Appointments distribute planned arrivals across the day. However, a service that takes longer than expected can delay several later appointments, and some people will arrive before their scheduled time. The system also determines what happens to someone who needs help but could not book. Providing a clearly identified way to handle that case can prevent the design from solving one visible queue by creating an invisible delay elsewhere. Measuring only the wait after a person reaches the desk would not capture the time spent waiting for a booking.

Fairness in a queue depends on the service and on the reasons for giving priority. A simple first-arrival rule is easy to explain when everyone is seeking the same thing. At a repair desk, however, a quickly completed collection might use a different process from an examination of a damaged item. Directing the two requests to different places can reduce interference without claiming that one person is more important. If a service does give priority to urgent cases, the criteria should be stated in a way that users can understand. People can then distinguish a deliberate exception from a system that is applying its rules unpredictably.

Measurements of waiting deserve the same attention as measurements of service. A person who leaves before reaching a desk may not appear in a record of completed cases. If the busiest queue causes the most people to leave, a calculation based only on completed cases could make the busiest period look better than it was. A survey can include observations of departures, or it can report that the recorded times apply only to people who were served. The writer favours recording both the experience of those who finish and evidence about those who leave, because each group provides information about a different aspect of access.

A successful change should be evaluated against a clear problem. Moving a desk can improve the use of space without changing how long a complicated request takes. Giving visitors a place to check forms before joining a line can shorten some service times without reducing the number of arrivals. Offering additional appointments can change when demand becomes visible. Each change addresses a different cause. A comparison before and after the change is most useful when it states which wait, for which group of visitors, was expected to improve. This preserves a connection between the design decision and the evidence used to judge it.
